newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Voting on Brazil civil service reform seen slow.
newsitem.headline: Voting on Brazil civil service reform seen slow.

text.p: Brazil's Chamber of Deputies was due to resume voting on amendments to the government's civil service reform bill this week, but there was little chance of the bill clearing the lower house before the end of May, said Giselle Artur, press aide to the government's chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies Benito Gama.
"The government knew civil service was going to be the toughest of the all the reforms and expected it to take some time," Artur said. "It affects the pockets of lots of people."
The Brazilian government sent its version of the civil service reform bill to Congress in August 1995.

A watered down version of the bill was approved on the floor of the lower house earlier this month by 309 votes, just one vote more than the three-fifths majority it needs as a constitutional amendment.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso then angered many deputies when he withdrew the government's support for an amendment which would have exempted lawmakers from a 10,800 real ($10,188) pay ceiling included in the reform.
With the lower house in uproar over the U-turn last week, the government managed to vote only two of more than 100 proposed amendments to the bill.
Artur said the government this week would continue putting forward only uncontroversial amendments to the bill, saving for later other amendments which strike at the heart of the reform.
However, many of the 100 outstanding amendments were identical or touched on similar clauses of the original bill and only nine would actually be put to a vote.
Even so, voting would be slow. Brazil's Chamber of Deputies effectively works a three-day week, with many members remaining in the home areas on Mondays and Fridays.
With the government requiring three-fifths majorities to defeat the amendments, it may opt to vote only on Wednesdays, the day when most lawmakers are present in the capital.

"There's a bank holiday in the week of May 1 so that's a week lost," said Artur. "Say we get the amendments finished a week later; then there'll be a couple of weeks before the bill is put to its final vote. We're looking at the end of May."
As a constitutional amendment, the bill requires two three-fifths majorities in each house of Congress. Once approved in the Chamber of Deputies, it would advance to the Senate.

Artur said whips felt the slow pace of voting was a price worth paying to avoid a repeat of last year's mauling of the government's pension reform bill, which had many of its key points defeated during voting on amendments.
The pension reform bill is currently being rewritten in the Senate. If approved there, the bill would go back to the Chamber of Deputies for approval of its new-look text.
